rationale: The psalm makes the speaker's tongue a swift scribe's reed. Baruch describes the corresponding literal movement from Jeremiah's mouth to a written document. The comparison explains the oral-writing image; it does not identify the psalm's speaker with either man or attribute this royal song to Jeremiah.

The royal addressee is told to gird a sword upon his thigh. The mighty men surrounding Solomon's couch each carry a sword upon the thigh against nocturnal terror. Both place this equipment within a royal setting, while the psalm addresses the warrior himself and the Song describes guards around a couch.

The psalm describes aromatic substances coming from the royal figure's garments; the Song praises the bride's fragrant garments and then names a garden's perfumes, including myrrh. These are related poetic uses of fragrance in descriptions of beloved figures, not an identification of the garments, persons or perfume recipes.

The king's daughter is arrayed in gold and varied embroidery. Ezekiel's personified woman receives patterned coverings, gold and silver, a crown and celebrated beauty. The shared adornment imagery illuminates the splendid clothing; it does not identify the daughter with Jerusalem or turn the psalm into the same allegory.

The psalm anticipates sons succeeding the fathers and being appointed rulers. Rehoboam appoints his son Abijah as ruler among his brothers with the intention of making him king. The narrative supplies a concrete father-to-son appointment, while the psalm's plural sons and worldwide rule exceed this particular appointment and are not identified with it.

The psalm warns against fear when another person grows rich; its following verse places that person's glory under death's limit. Proverbs warns a poor person against stretching to match a rich man and depicts the man disappearing from sight. Both restrain a response to another's wealth; Proverbs' pronouns are preserved rather than rewritten as wealth itself growing wings.

God's claim to own the animals explains, in the psalm's sacrificial discussion, why human offerings cannot supply something independently His worshipers own. David likewise says that everything offered for the holy house already belongs to God and came from His hand. The shared reasoning concerns divine ownership underlying worship, with animals in the psalm and building resources in Chronicles.

The psalm's troubled heart and dread of death stand beside Jesus' statement that His soul is troubled as He considers asking the Father for rescue from the approaching hour. John's surrounding discourse explicitly concerns His death. This is a comparison of articulated inward distress and appeal to God, not an identification of the psalmist or a claim that their responses are identical.

The psalm says ordinary enemy reproach would be bearable, before contrasting it with the close companion of verses 14-15. Micah warns against confidence in friends and intimate companions and describes enemies within the household. Both make breached closeness more disturbing than hostility from a recognized outsider; neither supplies the identity of the psalm's companion.

The psalm joins hostility toward the speaker's words with evil thoughts against him. Jeremiah's opponents explicitly devise a design against him and propose striking him with the tongue. The comparison concerns plotted, verbal hostility; Jeremiah's final clause says they will hear all his words, so it is not treated as a refusal to listen or as the same episode.

relationship: figurative refuge illustrated by a tower
rationale: Calling God a tower of strength before the enemy uses the defensive function shown at Thebez: inhabitants flee into a fortified tower while Abimelech attacks, and his assault fails. Judges supplies a concrete illustration of the refuge image, not the psalm's historical occasion or an assertion that its figurative tower is that building.

relationship: divinely imposed trap in communal lament
rationale: The psalm attributes entry into a trap and bodily affliction to God. Personified Jerusalem likewise attributes a net spread for her feet, being turned backward and continual pain to Him. The shared lament imagery joins divine agency, entrapment and suffering without identifying the community's ordeal with a particular captivity.

The psalm describes God's royal processions in the holy place, followed in context by musicians and an assembly. Samuel narrates the ark's joyful procession with dancing companies, instruments, shouting and trumpet. This is a comparison of ceremonial movement associated with God's presence; it does not establish that the psalm narrates David's particular procession.

relationship: appeal to God's knowledge of reproach
rationale: The psalm grounds its appeal in God's knowledge of the speaker's reproach and afflicters. Jeremiah asks the Lord to remember and vindicate him against pursuers and to know the reproach he received concerning Him. Both appeals bring persecution and reproach before God's knowledge, while Jeremiah's stated cause is not imposed on the unnamed psalmist.

The psalm asks that lawlessness be added to the enemies' lawlessness. Isaiah describes rebellious children making plans and agreements apart from God so as to add sins upon sins. The distinctive accumulation language is shared, but its agency differs: an imprecation addressed to God in the psalm and the rebels' own conduct in Isaiah.

The psalmist describes becoming like a portent to many while depending on God's help. Ezekiel is made a portent before Israel through actions subsequently explained as representing captivity. The comparison concerns a person being presented as a portent to observers; Ezekiel's explanation is not supplied as the meaning of the psalm's unexplained portent.

The psalm pictures mountains taking up peace for the people and hills in righteousness. Isaiah pictures mountains and hills leaping to welcome the people with joy. Both give the paired landforms an active role in a favorable communal scene; the differing actions remain intact, and neither landscape is converted into an identified set of human rulers.

relationship: wisdom reflection on the wicked's end
rationale: The psalmist's sanctuary insight concerns the last things of prosperous sinners, whose apparent security collapses in verses 18-20 like a dream. Zophar likewise describes the lawless person's apparent establishment ending in disappearance like a dream. This comparison follows the argument about deceptive prosperity; it neither identifies Job as wicked nor treats Zophar's accusation as a verdict on him.

relationship: wealth and the collapse of rest
rationale: The psalm places men of wealth and their empty hands beside troubled hearts and sleep. Job's discourse describes a rich man lying down, opening his eyes and being gone, with night and removal following. Wealth fails to secure enduring rest in both portrayals; the psalm's sleepers are not silently renamed slain warriors or identified with Job's rich man.

The psalm joins troubled, uncomprehending hearts, sleep and wealthy men finding nothing with their hands. Jesus' rich man plans repose on the strength of stored goods, but God calls him a fool and demands his soul that night. The parable develops the related warning that wealth cannot secure rest or possession; it is not asserted to narrate the psalm's event.

The psalm explicitly calls people to bow, fall and weep before their Maker. Nehemiah records the people bowing with faces to the ground and weeping as they hear the law. These bodily responses correspond, but the leaders then forbid mourning on that holy day; the narrative is not treated as an unqualified command to repeat the same response.

The psalm says God has not dealt with the community according to its sins. Nehemiah's confession recounts disobedience and being handed to foreign peoples, yet says abundant compassion prevented their complete destruction or abandonment. Both distinguish the people's wrongdoing from the merciful restraint of God's response; neither requires an absence of all punishment.

relationship: contrast in provision for wild animals
rationale: The psalm's springs supply drinking water to beasts and satisfy wild donkeys' thirst. Jeremiah's lack-of-rain scene has empty wells, failed pasture and wild donkeys whose eyes fail for lack of grass. The contrasting scenes show wild animals receiving or lacking provision; Jeremiah's stated grass deprivation is not changed into a claim that those donkeys died of thirst.

relationship: daylight as the time for work
rationale: The psalm sets human labor until evening within the alternation of day and nocturnal animal activity. Jesus uses the same day-and-night limit to urge the works of His sender while it is day, before the night when no one can work. The comparison links the ordinary daily pattern with its use in His explanation of urgent work, without equating their settings.

The speaker takes a cup of salvation in answer to what the Lord has done, within a thanksgiving and vow context. Psalm 22 praises the Lord's excellent, intoxicating cup alongside His provision and lasting mercy. The poems relate a cup to divine beneficence; this does not establish a shared ritual or identify either cup as the Eucharist.

The psalm asks how long the servant has and when God will judge his pursuers. Habakkuk asks how long his cry while wronged will go unanswered and describes judgment not reaching completion while the impious oppresses the righteous. Both articulate the distress of awaiting justice under oppression without identifying a common adversary or calculating a duration.

The psalmist asks when judgment against pursuers will come. Jesus' widow repeatedly asks a judge for justice against her adversary, and His application concerns God's chosen ones crying day and night for justice. The parable addresses the psalm's kind of waiting appeal; it supplies neither the servant's lifetime nor an identity for the persecutors.

The psalm connects not turning away from God's judgments with being instructed by Him. Isaiah's speaker receives the Lord's instruction through an opened ear and answers that he does not disobey or contradict. Both make divine teaching the setting for obedient response; Isaiah's actual wording is retained rather than replaced with an expected turned-back phrase.

The psalmist reckons the earth's sinners as transgressors and therefore loves God's testimonies. Paul explains that the law makes the world answerable to God and brings knowledge of sin. The connection concerns instruction exposing wrongdoing; Paul's argument about justification is not made identical to the psalmist's declaration of love, nor is the psalm said to quote Romans.

relationship: justice and rescue from the wrongdoer's hand
rationale: The psalmist claims judgment and righteousness and asks not to be handed to those who wrong him. Jeremiah's command joins doing justice and righteousness with rescuing the plundered from the wrongdoer's hand. The same cluster of just conduct and protection from an oppressor appears as a personal appeal and as a command to those responsible for justice.

The psalm describes their full storehouses and multiplying sheep. Deuteronomy's blessing catalogue likewise joins productive flocks with blessed storehouses and storerooms. These concrete prosperity images correspond; the psalm's preceding foreigners and ensuing distinction about happiness are preserved, so its owners are not declared obedient covenant recipients merely from their abundance.

relationship: contrast in the sound of public squares
rationale: The psalm's picture of their security includes no cry in their squares. Amos announces the opposite public condition: mourning in every square and road as the Lord passes through. The contrast concerns the audible sign of communal peace or distress, without identifying the psalm's prosperous group with the people addressed by Amos.

The psalm praises God for strengthening Jerusalem's gate bars and blessing children within her. Zechariah promises a populous Jerusalem with God as a wall of fire around her and glory within. Both join Jerusalem's inhabited interior to protection provided by God; the fiery wall is not turned into the psalm's literal bars or assigned to Nehemiah's gate orders.

relationship: the Lord's word pictured as running
rationale: The psalm says God's sent word will run swiftly. Paul requests prayer that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified. The unusual running image is shared, while the psalm's following weather and Israel-instruction context differs from Paul's request concerning proclamation; no direct quotation is claimed.

The psalm extends its praise summons across young men, young women, old and younger people. Joel's summons to a consecrated gathering deliberately includes elders, nursing infants, bridegroom and bride. Both make participation span age and household stages; Joel's fast and pleading are not identified with the psalm's praise occasion.

The psalm calls executing a written judgment glory for all God's holy ones. Paul says the saints will judge the world and angels and uses that expectation in discussing disputes. Both associate holy ones with judgment, but Paul does not identify the psalm's unnamed written judgment or prescribe its pictured weapons for church disputes.

relationship: judgment and honor of the holy ones
rationale: The psalm attaches glory for the holy ones to judgment against the hostile nations and rulers of its context. Daniel sees the horn attack the holy ones until the Ancient of Days gives judgment to them and they receive kingship. The shared association is judgment with their vindication and honor; the psalm's particular written judgment remains unidentified.
